opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that gap is really striking, and it's not that surprising if you've watched how technology diffuses historically. There's always a big lag between when something becomes technically possible and when it actually reshapes how businesses operate. Electricity took decades to really transform factory design, because you had to rethink the whole layout of the factory, not just swap out the steam engine for a motor.

With LLMs there's a similar dynamic, plus some factors specific to this technology. Current LLMs are remarkably capable in a broad but shallow way. They can do a huge range of things at a sort of competent-intern level. But they're also unreliable in ways that are hard to predict. They hallucinate, they lose the thread on complex multi-step tasks, and they don't have a solid grounding in what's true versus what merely sounds plausible. So if you're running a business process where errors are costly, whether in legal, medical, finance, or engineering, you can't just drop an LLM in and walk away. You need humans checking the output, you need to redesign workflows around the strengths and weaknesses of the tool, and that takes time, expertise and organizational willpower that most companies don't have lying around.

Then there's the human and institutional side. People are used to doing their jobs a certain way. Middle managers aren't always eager to automate their own teams. There are regulatory and liability questions nobody has fully worked out. And a lot of enterprises have messy data spread across legacy systems, so even if the model is smart enough, getting it the right context to act on is a big integration project.

So I'd say if you froze LLM capability exactly where it is now, there'd still be many years of economic absorption ahead, and a lot of value would get unlocked just by people figuring out how to use what's already there.

But I'd also add my usual caveat, which is that I don't think LLMs as they exist now are the path to AGI by themselves. They're a very powerful component, but they lack real reasoning grounded in a world model, they lack the ability to learn continuously from experience, and they lack the kind of self-reflective cognition you'd want in a genuinely general intelligence. Part of why adoption is slower than the hype suggested is that people intuitively bump into those limitations. When we get systems that combine neural pattern recognition with more explicit reasoning, memory and learning, which is what we're working toward with Hyperon and related architectures, I think a lot of those reliability barriers fall away, and the adoption curve could get much steeper very quickly. So the current gap is partly organizational inertia and partly a fairly accurate signal from the market about what these systems can and can't yet be trusted to do.

r001.rationale: The response names organizational inertia and institutional barriers, but does not clearly say AI is already capable of doing human jobs.

r002.rationale: It questions whether current LLMs can reach AGI because they lack grounded reasoning, continuous learning, and self-reflective cognition; it does not cite lack of creativity.

r003.rationale: The response makes no claim about minor modifications enabling LLMs to perform roughly 95% of human jobs.

r004.rationale: It does not claim that most jobs require little fundamental creativity or inventiveness.

r005.rationale: It discusses workflow redesign and integration, but not automating most work by matching tasks to recorded human activity.

r006.rationale: It does not discuss differing social reactions to automated versus human enforcement or automated stores.

r007.rationale: It predicts faster adoption when more reliable systems arrive, but does not argue that a sufficiently large capability or cost advantage can overcome social obstacles.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think there's a few different things going on there, and they're worth pulling apart. The first is just the ordinary lag you see with any transformative technology. Electricity took decades to actually reshape factories, because you had to re-architect the factory around it rather than just swap out the steam engine. LLMs are somewhat similar. You can drop ChatGPT into an existing workflow and get a modest productivity bump, but the big gains come when you redesign the whole business process around the fact that a lot of cognitive labor is now cheap. Most organizations haven't done that yet, and organizational change is slow for reasons that have nothing to do with the technology.

The second thing, which I think is underappreciated, is that these systems are genuinely unreliable in ways that matter for deployment. An LLM can write you a beautiful contract summary and then hallucinate a clause that doesn't exist. For a lot of economically valuable tasks, being right ninety percent of the time is not good enough, and the cost of checking the output starts to eat the savings. So there's a real gap between impressive demo and dependable tool, and that gap is partly about the lack of real understanding in these systems. They're interpolating over a massive training corpus rather than reasoning from a grounded model of the world, and that shows up precisely in the edge cases that enterprises care about.

And then the third piece is more sociological and economic. A lot of the people who'd be displaced by this technology are also the people who'd have to implement it, and there's some natural resistance there. Regulatory and liability questions are unresolved. And frankly, the incentives of the big AI companies are to sell subscriptions and API calls, not necessarily to do the hard, unglamorous integration work in a mid-sized insurance company in Ohio.

So my view is that the capability is ahead of the deployment by a fair margin, maybe several years, but I'd also caution against assuming the current architectures will close that gap on their own. I think getting to the kind of robust, trustworthy cognition that actually gets woven into the economy at scale is going to require going beyond pure transformer-based LLMs toward more hybrid systems that combine neural learning with symbolic reasoning, with actual goal structures and memory. That's the direction we've been pushing with OpenCog Hyperon. In the meantime, you'll see uneven adoption: fast in software development and content generation where errors are cheap and easy to catch, much slower in medicine, law, and finance where they aren't.

r001.rationale: It identifies slow organizational change and resistance from workers who would need to implement the technology as barriers, while describing LLM capability as ahead of deployment.

r002.rationale: It discusses reliability and lack of grounded understanding, but does not attribute skepticism about human-level AGI to a lack of fundamental creativity.

r003.rationale: It gives no estimate that LLMs with minor modifications could perform roughly 95% of human jobs.

r004.rationale: It does not claim that most human jobs require little fundamental creativity or inventiveness.

r005.rationale: It does not explain automating work by matching tasks to previously recorded human activity.

r006.rationale: It does not discuss automated stores or different reactions to automated versus human enforcement.

r007.rationale: It does not argue that a large enough capability or cost advantage would overcome social barriers to adoption.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a substantial gap, because what’s technically possible and what’s actually integrated into the economy are two quite different things. You can demonstrate that an LLM does a useful task in a few minutes. Getting that capability into a company’s workflow, connected to its data, with someone responsible for checking the output—that can take a lot longer.

And the unevenness of these systems matters. A model can do something quite sophisticated and then make a mistake that seems absurdly elementary. If you’re using it to brainstorm, that’s fine. If you’re putting it into a process where an error costs a lot of money, you need checks around it. The economic question becomes: how much does it cost to make this useful and dependable in this particular setting?

So I wouldn’t interpret slow adoption as evidence that the capabilities have no economic value. There’s a lot of organizational adaptation involved. Businesses have existing software, existing procedures, people who know how to do things a certain way. Those don’t change instantly because a new model comes out.

Even if the technology stopped improving for a while, I think we’d still see substantial impact as people worked out how to use what already exists. But of course it isn’t stopping, so organizations are trying to adapt to something that keeps changing underneath them.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a pretty substantial gap, because having a system that can do something in a demo is quite different from integrating it into an actual business process. A lot of economic activity is embedded in these complicated networks of software, human relationships, organizational habits, and regulations. You can’t just drop an LLM into that and expect everything to reorganize itself overnight.

And the limitations matter. If a system does a task well most of the time, that can be tremendously useful when a person is checking its work. But if you want it to carry out a whole sequence of actions autonomously, those occasional errors can compound. So there’s work to do around reliability, connecting systems to the right data and tools, and figuring out where human oversight belongs.

I suspect we could get a lot more economic impact from the capabilities we already have, even without another fundamental breakthrough. But adoption takes time, and meanwhile the technology keeps moving. So you have these two processes running at different speeds: what the AI can potentially do, and what institutions have actually figured out how to use it for.
